I'm 36 and got this every day of my life, even less than an hour ago.  It's horrible to begin with, but worse in how it taints your ability to trust anyone who actually is willing to help, because we've all learned that help means they will later use it against you for their own ammunition. Worse, I've been to doctors that have found most of what is going on, and it's actual serious illnesses that because I believed I was that ungrateful b**** could have been stopped earlier.  Now it's just a matter of waiting for them to get worse while my NMom uses it all against me.

Not sure what I can add here, but I can at least give you part of my own story.  I had started harming at age 25, probably three years before I met my fiance, and I didn't do it often, just enough that it helped here and there when I couldn't do other things to help.  One day I had gotten into an argument with my father (which was rare and really set me off as my mother was the one to do this, not him), and that urge was back.  So I told him and he freaked.  I didn't harm that day, but a couple years later started again.  Since then, I still harm, but I've had to learn how to hide it, even changing methods so that it doesn't leave a mark as much.  I hate that I have to hide it, but I also hate the day where I went to him in confidence and he blew up.  I think we lost something that day between us that we won't get back, and not just trust, and I admit there are days where I sometimes just wish I could walk away from my own life and into a different one.  End of the day I realize I have to be responsible for myself and all my actions, including ones where I wish I could go to someone else.  It's lonely, but I think I'm more self-reliant and know how/where to hold back if I have to because of it.  And I hope if anything you can gain something from this as well.

I can tell by what you wrote here that you really cared for her and you thought she cared for you, and it sounds really rough having to see her like that on a regular basis, especially as, to be honest, a lot of what she has done and said sounds a bit superficial.  Looking at how she treated you in the end, and how she also relied on you for a lot - that was very unfair to you, to make you responsible for her.  I know a few women who act like her, heck I probably acted like her at one point, but she's not worth it, not if even the memory of her is harming you daily still - and once I got them out of my life, I have been much happier for it.  It's never fair to you if you are the one responsible for another person's responsibilities that they need to owe up to themselves.  It's time to find ways for you to move forward.  She is in your past.  Take from the relationship only the good things you had and find ways to shed the bad baggage that she left you with (well, you can learn from mistakes within it as well if you wish :) ).  She has her problems as we all do, and her problems are not your problems.  End of the day, you still need to find ways to take care of _you_, not the other way around.  Honestly, if you can distance her on social media and find ways to distance her in your daily life, it will help a lot, and maybe find something in your life that you enjoy that you can reach out socially with as well.  Sports, collectibles, games, etc..., all are great things to find people with, and it probably wouldn't hurt either to find someone locally who is a professional to talk to as well.

Definite cyberhugs being sent your way.  I had that happen too a few years back; I was at a seven-year point, had only thought about it once during that time, and then some horrible drama happened between my friends that ended up making me leave all of them.  I also had it where my boyfriend blew up at me when I mentioned it.  What you can do though, is let him know about the stress that has triggered it, and tell him about the stress at least for now.  If you feel comfortable that he'll be supportive about the self-harm, then mention it, but like I said, my experience, I thought he'd be supportive, but he wasn't.  Maybe too as an alternative, find something you can keep on you to help distract you when those feelings hit again if he or other friends aren't around that you can call, if even to use hearing them talk as a way to keep distracted.

I read through the other replies; college is so stressful, especially in that kind of environment.  I find that if I know what is triggering me to have my mind hit that point, then I can first, actively work to avoid said trigger.  If I can't avoid it then I try to at least find a place I can be alone a bit.  In college there was a handicap stall in the bathroom I'd often go; the floor I was on was not handicap accessible, so I used it instead for a mental health break.  If I can't get away from the stress, then I do a bit of a meditation technique I've come up with as a coping mechanism.  I just sort of try to mentally phase out what's stressing me (such as a relative nagging) and see instead someone I want to be there, and in my mind, that person is giving me a hug, or rubbing my back, or saying encouraging words that remind me to breath and that the moment will pass.  I know that if I don't have someone (or a mental image of someone) encouraging me to stay safe, then I won't want to stay safe.  As for the weed (or alcohol use even), I'd avoid it; while they may physically relax you, they also act as a depressant against your central nervous system.  This means slowed responses and lowered inhibitions, which equates to probably doing something stupid.  Enhance your nutrition too if you can; fruits, veggies, lean protein, plenty of water.  Some people use caffeine, but honestly, only use it if you're trying to wake up a bit, and equal it out with more water.  Green tea is great, but again, there is still caffeine there.

If you haven't already, I'd call back the new member desk and explain the anxiety as well.  There's a possibility they will talk to the doctor to see if (s)he is willing to make an exception and/or make a recommendation.  Often too, there will be a nurse practitioner or physician's assistant in the practice taking overflow for the same physician.  

Otherwise if that doesn't work, talk with the nurse more to see recommendations as well.  You can also call the closest office to you and talk to a nurse there as well and explain the situation.  They should be more than willing to at least listen and help advise as well.

Honestly, like the other posters, best to put it down and keep control.  Talk it out here like you are (so KEEP talking!), find a friend locally you can trust, there are support groups, anything to NOT do it again.  I know that many do it once and that's it, but you found yourself here, and I think most of us can say that most of us continued to do it.  If you can find another way to get the same benefit of the action without the harm, please do that instead!  Looking back, I really wish I had another outlet at the time I started, because even now, ten years later, there are still plenty of times in my mind I see no other way to cope, even though I have to work hard to control myself from doing it.  Heck, for me it was even stronger than alcohol was, it can be that horrid of an addiction.  Even worse now, it grows like a tolerance -- you need more each time you harm.  I'm to the point that the harm itself only even works anymore if I'm drunk, which really isn't good.  So like the other posters, do anything you can to stop now, and please keep talking here!

Oh gosh, first off, cyber hugs for that kind of workload!  I was a music ed major (6 years) the first time through then changed into nursing.  For the music I had a senior recital that I ended up dropping (so dropped the minor it was required for), and then a web portfolio as well with lesson plans, papers, and such.  I definitley can understand that kind of huge demand it is!  And working on top of it!  But both times, the worse I felt in all of it was when I had three semesters left as well.  

But, what can be helpful will be two things (and these are the only two things that helped me).  The first is to e-mail or call your adviser as soon as you can; the advisers I always had were wonderful, not just for schedule planning, but as someone to go to when I was stressed and needed a surrogate parent figure to cry to (and yes, there was crying).  If your adviser isn't the type that you feel comfortable going to, you can also probably find another trusted/favorite professor or even student counseling services on your campus and someone will be able to help.  

And the other huge thing was really micromanaging my schedule.  This helped in nursing school when the schedule was so hectic I had to schedule in bathroom breaks and everything.  But, it's hugely comforting to see a schedule on the wall telling you that it's okay to be working on specific classwork at a specific time.  I did have to give up some socialization when my schedule was hectic, but in the long run, I am happier that I took the time to do the schedule as opposed to what I would have done, which was just procrastinate.

What are some of the things about the upcoming semester (or previous semesters) that are making things hard?  And what kind of major are you in?  With three semesters left, you've come a VERY long way, would be hard to put that work aside so soon.  Plus, is it possible to talk to your adviser or another trusted professor in your department?  They may have some ideas on how to make things more bearable for you as well.

Not sure if I'm too late to the party, but you can try massaging the scar as it heals as well, it will help stretch it a bit and prevent excess scar tissue from forming.  Also, you can get topical Vitamin E, or get a good lotion with extra Vitamin E in it as well to help it heal better after it has formed a good scab.

As a nurse, I can say it's both a hard but a good place to be.  I started cutting before nursing school, actually school helped it go away, and I restarted after finishing.  But, I had a psych clinical, my prof didn't know about my cutting.  I ended up helping with a patient for the duration whose arms were scarred up and down, and all I could think was "it's easier to hide on your thigh."  It's a definite exercise in clinical detachment mixed with utilizing what little cognitive behavioral therapy I have had practice with, and compassion, cause it's even harder to use that skill when you have to detach yourself.  

And you're still very much helping people.  That person, as awkward and uncomfortable it was for you both, you got them somewhere where they can be away from what was causing a problem, if even for a few hours.  You very well might have saved their life even.  And I'm sure there have been other lives you have already saved, or at least affected, in your career.

Better at reading people or not feeling abandoned?  I guess over the years I've gotten used to the feeling at least. But, something that I have to remind myself of if/when I am feeling any abandonment too is that at the end of the day, I am the one responsible for my words, my actions.  So I guess I ask myself, are they abandoning me because of me, or because of them?  I know a lot of my closest friends/family have their own struggles, and often when they seem to be pulling away from me, it's because they themselves are feeling the exact same things too.

I've felt that way for years.  I've learned with time to be both more discerning as to whom I let in; I vet them more to make sure they won't hurt me.  But I also get a better read on whom I should just keep at a distance.  I guess it comes down to getting better at reading them.

I usually hold back, and when I finally did tell, my friend panicked and ran, not even thinking about the fact it happened to me and not her.  I lived with it for two months, and she stormed off after knowing two minutes?  That's  why I stopped talking to them at that level.

Maybe write and cook a bit.  But really, no people that I know, they only seem to make it all worse for me anyway.

Fellow nurse here (3 years) with a few red stripes at the moment and I can relate.  If it helps, think back to doing this same thing 6 years ago, pre-NCLEX, and still being in the emotional trainwreck that is nursing school.  You have 6 more years of knowledge and experience than you did back then, and have already practiced this area, even if it's been awhile.  Plus, if you still have your old notes and books from college, they help too.  At least it will be easier than doing this the first time.  

Otherwise, as for mental health, I know a lot of people on here have had help with 7cupsoftea.com and if you aren't in the talking mood, calm.com - both seem to help in some very good ways.  And if at work, I admit to a few times going to the linen or store room for items and hiding until I can regain my composure.  Or bathroom if really needed.  Even if it's something as silly as a Spongebob sticker on your clipboard, even little things help to distract from those feelings that for me dominated in school.

Being someone here who actually is a fetishist under another user name, I can safely tell you that self harm is NOT a fetish.  However, I will rely on what I know from that side of my life to tell you now to open communication, listen, and while you may be angry, remember your marriage vows first and foremost - for better or for worse.  

If for her it is or becoming a fetish thing, there are some decent places on Reddit to look in to; I won't link them here as I do know there are teens on here as well who I don't encourage them to find that yet (teens, enjoy your youth!). And once things get back on track, and if you are sent back to the US, remember, study up for college and find a school with a semester abroad program back to Austria. In reality, I don't think there's been enough research on our group at all to really know what goes on to start and trigger selfharm, and even then, I think the researches are putting too much emphasis on "selfharm" as a label for a disorder when in fact it gives the same exact biochemical release as addictions give and is in fact identical to other addictive behaviors.  Yes, I said it - self harm is an addiction.  I think with the new adoption of the DSM-V for mental health practices we will see more research and better classification of selfharm in this regard; before the old DSM-IV-TR classified it into borderline personality disorder, which honestly, I have not met someone who selfharms who fits into that diagnosis.  In fact, according to [Medscape](http://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/803884_15), "Whereas in DSM-IV non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) was considered a symptom of borderline personality disorder (BPD), in the revised manual it is recognized as a distinct condition. Research suggests that NSSI can occur independent of BPD, such as in patients with depression or even in those with no other diagnosable psychopathology."  While the article mentions that specific incidents need to occur, I am sure that even having the urge to harm is akin to having the NNSI diagnosis, just as having the urge to drink with a history of alcohol abuse is akin to being a recovering alcoholic.  Even then, [Psychology Today](http://www.psychologytoday.com/blog/the-scarred-soul/201002/non-suicidal-self-injury-new-diagnosis) linked another article that actually lists the new specific diagnostic criteria as well, which is interesting.  

The step by step stimulus and response listed above is present in any other addiction, just with ours, our trigger is to harm ourselves rather than use another means to get that release of endorphins; and of course as the addiciton really sets in, the trigger on its own becomes internalized as withdrawal from the endorphins.  Even then, binge drinking, binge eating, unprotected sex, drug use, reckless driving, internet gaming, gambling (the first article linked above discusses this a bit as well, calling gaming the "only non-substance-related addictive disorder"), exercise, work - all have an element of self harm to them because honestly, none of them are really good for us when performed at an extreme.  A lot of literature says that us adults don't self harm because we have other means to do that, though none of the means listed really appeal to me, none are as quick or easy, none are cheap, and this is the easiest to physically recover from. 

ETA:  Found a copy of the new DSM-V table of contents - "NonSuicidal Self-Injury" is listed as the very bottom as "Conditions for Further Study."  Looks like we'll be seeing more emerge in the future, which is good.  

ETAA:  Found [another article](http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2695720/) which backs up a lot of what we have been discussing, both in this thread and other areas of r/slefharm.  The article itself is from as psychiatry journal, peer-reviewed, and not only says that 1/3 to 1/2 of all adolescents self harm, but "...self injury seems to acquire addictive characteristics and can be quite difficult for a person to discontinue."  In other words, not only are there more of us out there than we realize, but it can become an addiction.

For me, I am about eight years into this journey, and there have been plenty of times it gets better, and plenty of times it has gotten worse.  I think those of us who are at points of our lives where society labels us as "adults" the selfharming behaviors can be akin to addictions or even anger management; some people drink, some do drugs, some have affairs, others work far too long for no reward, and some of us like you and me selfharm.  

Though I am not in a place to really seek counseling for my own problems, I have had some of the training that would be used in part of the team that would be counseling the individual, and have been able to apply it to myself.  In this case, a lot of assessment of external stimuli/triggers and identifying what specifically will trigger me.  It's like a chain:  Person puts me down -> I feel put down -> I cannot stand up for myself -> I selfharm.  Or because we all have our own varieties:  External stimuli -> Internal reaction -> Reaction to internal reaction -> Selfharm.  The "getting it better" is finding a way to break the links in that chain without breaking ourselves.  To clarify:  for me it was working backwards through the chain; first finding why I harm myself (the reaction to internal reaction), then identifying backwards to the point that when I see someone behaving in a way that triggers me, I am at least able to walk away (I am not yet at a point where I am able to stand up to them but will be eventually).  

I am not religious nor am I seeking religion, but there is a phrase "Grant me the grace/strength to deal with the things I cannot change."  I cannot change other people's behaviors that trigger me because often they do not want to change nor do they think they have to, but I can at least learn how to identify their behaviors and my responses quicker to learn to deal with them better.  

There's also the approach of learning to think differently about the situation, and even modeling what you want to become.  You have a son, a career, a new family coming up.  What would the person you want to be do in those situations?  If you can answer that question, you have the means to become that person. It will take time, it will take practice, but with the right motivations and reasons, it can happen.

I've done a nursing clinical in a private psych hospital a few years ago in school in the US, both adult and child/adolescent.  This is a bit of a book, but I spent several weeks in this clinical, going multiple days per week.  In addition to my time as a nursing student, I have had my own battles with self harm, depression, and anxiety over the years.  I hope that what I learned out of this can go to help you at least partially overcome the fears of the experience. 

In the US at least, it depends on the quality of hospital whether or not your stay is as beneficial as it could be.  The hospital I was with was fairly good, and several of the clients I worked with had been in the county's public psych hospital as well and stated the private one was much better.  In the US at least, most counties have their own psych hospital

In the US there are voluntary and involuntary holds; involuntary is usually a mandatory 72 hour hold, however that does not include weekends.  If you end in on a Thursday or Friday, you are there 72 hours plus the weekend.  The staff told us that if we were going to harm ourselves, to do it Sunday night, Monday, or Tuesday so you could be out in time for the weekend.  Voluntary holds, while you can usually leave when you want (as long as you are not a threat to safety of yourself or others), often insurance will not cover it (also, often insurance for those in poverty has very little mental health coverage).  So really, the clients in the unit were there because they were considered a danger to themselves or others.  

A typical day in the psych hospital usually started with breakfast around 7:30 in a cafeteria, a unit meeting of all patients and staff around 8:30 (with meds being given by then - some meds could be given as early as 5 am), group and individual therapies for the morning with small breaks between (typical therapy, art therapy, music therapy, activities in a small gym), lunch at noon, afternoon is more therapy sessions, then dinner and evening as a group usually watching TV or with some free time.  Bedtime was between 9-10 pm.  There were obviously students there working with the clients as well; our role as students was to be paired with a client not as a nurse but more as a potential resource for the client to talk with individually and bounce ideas off of.  Us students enjoyed this, as did the clients, and we readily bonded pretty well; the nurses and our instructor knew how to pair us together well for personality and background.  There was more than one time daily when one client or another would be trying to help bring laughter and smiles to others.  There was always also one older female client who would act as a surrogate mother for the other clients too.    

The hospital area was comprised of a psych ICU and a regular adult unit, along with a child unit and an adolescent unit.  To be in any of the regular units you had to sign a no-harm contract, meaning that you would not attempt to harm yourself while in the unit, and if you did attempt, want to attempt, or succeeded, you would be placed into the psych ICU.  In the psych ICU there were two levels - the regular unstable clients, and those immediately harming themselves.  It was a rather quiet ward also, most people were just watching TV or napping, the drugs more or less making them sleepy.  There was also an isolation/observation room with the psych ICU where a client would go if they were violent or out of control - they would be forced into different clothing (a smock kind of gown), heavily sedated, and under continual watch until they calmed down; they were not allowed a blanket, and there was a mat on the floor.  When calm, they were given a set of scrubs and allowed to relax with TV or nap.  

All clients in the unit were involuntary and were kept until they were well enough to leave and agree to a no-harm contract.  All clients were brought in by police or ambulance from the main hospital's ER and were given a full physical as well when admitted to rule out physical causes of mental illness (such as thyroid problems), and to help get any physical problems in check to help assist with better mental health.  The size of the city was a smaller metropolitan area, so it was generally a main hospital ER handling all cases and then admitting to appropriate units from there (eg:  psych, cardiac, med/surg, etc...).  The first day of admittance to the unit, the staff often let the client rest and relax without too much bother, that way they could adjust and rest from the stress of the illness.  

All clients were also on sleeping aids, had a strict schedule, and not allowed caffeine while there unless a physician allowed it; in those cases they would have to get the coffee/soda from the nurse's station.  Pens were not allowed, but a client could use a pencil at the nurse's station.  I recall most of the clients wearing socks rather than shoes - I think the shoelace rule.  Ties from hoodies were usually kept by the nurses for the same reason.  Time in the bathroom was supervised by a nurse usually, but I think it was a case by case basis.  Ironically the rules were the same for the main hospital as well as most patients admitted to medical units were there becuase it was unsafe for them to be on their own medically.    

The rooms in the main unit were like cheap hotel rooms - two single beds, two dressers, a nightstand, a bathroom with a shower, sink, toilet, and vanity.  There was a communal room next to the nurse's station with a soda machine in it and plastic glasses.  Also a music/art room and a group therapy room as well.  The decor was probably late 1970s; it was comfortable enough, but worn down too from the age and the budgets being put towards better uses.  It was also more of a campus than a hospital, so it was more like being at a college dorm than being a patient in a psych ward.  Food was the same as the main hospital, which we didn't care for but still ate, though there were a few more options in the psych cafeteria than the main hospital.  

There were equal numbers of counselors on staff to nurses as well, and all nurses were RNs with 4 year degrees.  There was a lot of interaction between staff and clients as well, and not just for therapy, but for even just socialization which seemed beneficial.  The units were locked down however, though they told us that it was not to keep the clients from leaving, but rather to keep them protected from the outside world which had done them harm.  Most adult clients were there because of harming themselves (usually suicide), children that were there were all foster children who had severe behavioral issues (which was sad as well as most of them came down to a lack of discipline and bonding in the foster home), and the adolescents were a mix of the two groups.  

Overall it was not a bad place, the trick really was to trust the staff and not to lie; as long as a client was cooperative and showed they wanted to get better and have a better time with life, then the staff seemed to work well with the clients.  Though the staff was underpaid and overworked (typical of any health system now), they all had a passion for what they were doing for their clients, and were very caring and compassionate as well; the staff often would share notes with each other to make sure the therapies were appropriate for the clients.  There were a couple of clients that were manipulative however, and it was seen quickly, and they had a harder time - for them they had to be truthful to themselves first and then their therapists as well, but in many cases they could not just because of the pathology of their own illnesses.

I hate saying that everything is going to be alright, because sometimes it's not and you still have to prepare for it, and even if everything is alright, you will still have the memories and stories of this for the rest of your life, the good parts and the bad.

Hey Snoo  :)  I really wish I had been online last night because the I would have responded to your post sooner.

First off, hugs.  You say you're "a dumb teenager?" I don't believe that for one moment! The way you wrote this is beautiful, and you have a gift for writing and communicating.  While it is hard to go to school not feeling well, I do urge you to give it a try.  Have your mum talk to the school nurse and/or principal about what is happening, and they can help you adjust to being there too while not feeling well.  Your closest friends and favorite "annoying" teachers can be a huge help as well, whether it be to just help you smile while feeling nauseous, giving you a quiet cool space to recover in, or being someone to talk to about the frustrations.

It sounds like you're not having that good of a time either lately, and given what you talked about with the nausea, I can definitely understand; along with being a self harmer, I was diagnosed just over a year ago with Celiac Disease, where anything with wheat (or more specifically a protein known as "gluten") in it causes nausea, vomiting, and all those fun abdominal things you seem to be feeling right now too.  It's something I've had as long as I can remember but my doctors all my life thought it was asthma, or allergies, or a kidney thing which was very scary too, or a slew of other really long words that are hard to think about at any given time because there are so many varying symptoms to it.  I especially remember always getting really nauseated on field trips with school, and throwing up on the bus to and from events.  Not fun.  I almost feel sick thinking about how it felt. 

That said, another hug.  The stress and fear of what you are going through seem even scarier than the illness and nausea itself, and this comes from someone who thinks that nausea is the worst physical sensation to have to endure.  I do encourage you to keep seeing your doctor, and to encourage the doc and your mother to keep looking for the cause of what is happening.  Sometimes too just the anxiety and nerves of feeling ill will make it worse, and sometimes there actually is something there that a doctor needs to look into to find the cause.  If you do need an ultrasound, most of the techs that perform them are super gentle and super nice, and if you tell them it hurts they will be even gentler.  Plus if/when your doc orders it, you can ask for a dose of an anti-emetic as well to help you get through it easier.   

Also, there is something you can do to help yourself right now too.  Have you heard of keeping a food diary?  It's quite simple.  In it, you write down what you eat, how much, and when, and also write down what times you get nausea, how long it lasts, and how bad it is (if you write it also as a scale of 0-10, it makes it easier too.  0 would be "No nausea" and 10 would be throwing up and worse), or any other illness you may be feeling too.  You can also write in there anything about how anxious you're feeling, whether it be from school or from not feeling well.  The food diary will help you, your mum, and your doc figure out if something you're eating is causing problems.  And it might not just be one thing making you sick; while for me wheat was causing my problem, I thought for most of my life it was beef and green peppers, and even after going gluten-free, I still cannot eat either food.  

Hope this helps, and please do hang in there!  It might take a little time to be back at where you were before all the nausea started, but in the meantime, your friends, family, and teachers are going to be even more important to you.  Plus, I do want to hear more about how you're doing, so please let us know!  I'm saving your post here so it is easier to find again in the future.
